description_full: Daifuku Co., Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, provides consulting, engineering, design, manufacture, installation, and after-sales services for material handling systems, car wash machines, and other related equipment in Japan and internationally. The company offers storage, transport, sorting, and picking systems to distributors and manufacturers, including e-commerce, retailers, wholesalers, transportation, and warehousing customers, as well as to food, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals manufacturers. It also provides cleanroom transport and storage systems for the manufacturing of semiconductors and flat panel displays; systems for automobile production line systems; airport solutions, including baggage handling systems, automated baggage check-in systems, baggage screening systems, and software and controls; car wash machines and related products to filling stations and automobile dealers; and industrial computers, measuring/control systems, and IoT solutions. The company was formerly known as Daifuku Machinery Works Co., Ltd. and changed its name to Daifuku Co., Ltd. in 1984. Daifuku Co., Ltd. was incorporated in 1937 and is headquartered in Osaka, Japan.

financial_summary: Daifuku Co., Ltd. is a large-cap industrials business with a $10.9B market cap on $4.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 10% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 19% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $733M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
